attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that they are welcome to use different images or variable names in this project. They can click the palette to change the image.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Notice there is already code in the editor; there are four blank image variables under the comment // sprite images. Select aquatic images for each variable from the gallery or My Assets, then update the variable name accordingly. 


Underneath this starter code, add comments with these descriptions to the project: array set up, game set up, on A button pressed.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare 2 new arrays and type the image variable names inside the brackets [ ] for one, and image variable names as strings for the other?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of values are stored in the oceanImages array?

❓ What type of values are stored in the oceanStrings array?

❓ Why might it be useful to create 2 arrays with the same element names, but different element types?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that when creating multiple arrays with corresponding elements, it’s useful to use names that describe their type. This makes it easier to pull the right type of data from the corresponding array.

💡 In this project, the 2 arrays will be used to check a user inputted string and make something happen to the corresponding sprite image.
steps.instructions:
Create two arrays to store the variables as both images and strings!


Underneath // array set up, use the keyword let to declare a new array called oceanImages. Type an assignment operator, then use a pair of brackets [ ] to contain the elements in the array. 


Inside the brackets [ ], type the names of the 4 sprite image variables declared under // sprite images separated by commas. The code might look like:

let oceanImages = [starfish, octopus, fish, turtle] 

Follow the same steps to create a second array, called oceanStrings. In this array, type the names of the 4 sprite image variables again. Place quotation marks around each variable’s name, so that they are stored as string values. 


Now, the 4 sprite image variables are stored in the oceanImages array as image values and in the oceanStrings array as string values.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add use a for loop to create multiple sprites in the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the Player and hiding sprites be used for?

❓ How many times will the for loop run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a for loop has 3 expressions, separated by semicolons: initialization, run condition, and increment. Based on the default expressions, the for loop will run 5 times.

💡 Make sure the ninja keeps the hiding sprite’s image parameter blank. It will be updated in the next step using values from an array.
steps.instructions:
Add multiple sprites to the project! 


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // game set up. Update the sprite name and select the scuba diver image from My Assets. Use the default SpriteKind parameter: SpriteKind.Player.


Open Loops and drag [for] below the Player sprite’s code. Use the default expressions: 

let i = 0; i < 5; i++

Open Sprites again and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop. Update the sprite name to hidingSprite, and leave the image parameter blank. 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite appear in the center of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace img`...` in the sprites.create function with code that will pull an element from the oceanImages array depending on the counter variable’s index?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the sprites.create code know which value to pull from the oceanImages array?

❓ How many times will the for loop run? What happens on each iteration?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how oceanImages[i] is used in the image parameter of the sprites.create code. Each time a sprite is created, the element from the oceanImages array with an index that matches the current value of the loop’s counter variable is pulled. 

💡 The first time the for loop runs, the first element in the oceanImages array (0) will be used as the first sprite’s image. Both the counter variable and index will increase by 1 each time the for loop runs. Because the loop begins running at 0 and continues running while the counter variable is less than the length of the oceanImages array (4), the loop will run 4 times.
steps.instructions:
Code the loop to create 4 hiding sprites with images from an array, then place them in random positions!


Inside the run condition expression of the for loop, replace 5 by typing oceanImages, a dot operator, and selecting the length property from the code completion tool. Because the length of the array is 4, the for loop will run 4 times, beginning at 0, and continuing to run while the counter variable is less than the length of the oceanImages array.


Use the for loop’s counter variable to pull an image variable from the array. Replace img`...` with oceanImages and a pair of brackets [ ] with the i counter variable typed inside. Each time the loop runs, it will pull the sprite image at the index, or location, of the i counter variable from the oceanImages array, so that 4 different sprite images appear on screen.


Place each hiding sprite in a random position. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] inside the for loop. Update the sprite name and use randint to randomize the x and y-positions.


Click ▶ to see the 4 sprite images from the oceanImages array appear in random positions!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare the type of the empty oceanSprites array after the colon :?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

 ❓ Why does the type need to be defined when creating an empty array? 

❓ What symbols need to be included when declaring an empty array?

❓ What happens after each hiding sprite is created?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that an array can be made up of image, string, number, or sprite values. However, all elements in the array must be of the same type. As a result, it’s important to define what type of elements the empty array will store, so that the program is unable to add different types of elements into the same array.

💡 Make sure the ninja has included a colon :, the type Sprite, and a pair of brackets [ ] before the assignment operator in the oceanSprites array declaration code. Point out to the ninja that the Sprite type appears in teal and has a capital S.

💡 Explain to the ninja that each time a hiding sprite is created, its value is pushed to the end of the oceanSprites array. These elements will be able to be referenced later in the project.
steps.instructions:
Use an empty array to store the sprites created by the for loop!


Underneath // array set up, use the keyword let to declare an array called oceanSprites. When creating an array without an initial value, its type must be declared by typing a colon, the type, and a pair of brackets [ ] after its name. Since oceanSprites will contain sprites, use : Sprite[] after the array name. Then, type an assignment operator and a second pair of brackets [ ]. 


Inside the curly brackets { } of the for loop, type the name of the empty array, a dot operator, and select the push function from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses ( ), and the name of the hiding sprite inside, so that the code looks like: 

oceanSprites.push(hidingSprite)

Now, as the loop creates the hiding sprites, they are pushed, or added, to the oceanSprites array. They will be stored in the order that they are added.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a for element of loop and set it to run for each element of the oceanSprites array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is a for element of loop similar and different to a for loop? What did it look like in the blocks editor?

❓ What might happen to every element in the oceanSprites array?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that both the for element of and for loops run a chunk of code for a set number of times. However, a for loop uses the index to make something happen to specific elements in an array, whereas for element of loops perform actions on every element in an array, regardless of their index. 

💡 In a for element of loop, an element variable is used to cycle through each element in an array. The keyword represents the current element in the loop.

💡 In the next step, a sprite flag will be used to make something happen to every element in the oceanSprites array.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to pause briefly, then make something happen to all of the elements in an array!


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] underneath the for loop. Update the parameter so that the user has enough time to look at the sprites on screen, before they disappear.


Below the pause code, add a for element of loop by typing the keyword for, a pair of parentheses ( ) and a pair of curly brackets { }, so that the code looks like: for ( ) { }


Inside the parentheses, type the keyword let to declare an element variable called creature. After, type the keyword of then the name of the oceanSprites array.


The for element of loop will run 1 time for each element of the oceanSprites array and will perform the same action on each element, regardless of its index.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the Invisible sprite flag and set it to true inside the for element of loop so that all the hiding sprites disappear after the project pauses?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the setFlag function do? What did this look like in the blocks editor?

❓ Why is the element variable creature used as the sprite name in the setFlag code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that in the blocks editor, they used the [set sprite [auto destroy]] block to set sprite flags. In both editors, there are several sprite flags that the ninja can use to create certain effects for different sprites. In this example, sprite flags are used to make sprites turn “invisible” for a certain amount of time.

💡 Make sure the ninja has used the element variable creature as the sprite name in the setFlag code so that every element in the oceanSprites array becomes invisible after the project pauses.
steps.instructions:
Set the hiding sprites to disappear after the project pauses!


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] inside the curly brackets { } of the for element of loop. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

mySprite.setFlag
(SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy, false)

The setFlag function takes 2 parameters: flag and on. The flag parameter designates the sprite flag used, and the on parameter turns the sprite flag on or off. 


Replace mySprite with the element variable creature, then update the flag parameter by deleting .AutoDestroy. Retype the dot operator to view all of the sprite flag options. Select Invisible from the code completion tool. Set the on parameter to true so that the sprite flag is turned on when the for element of loop runs.


Click ▶ to see the hiding sprites disappear after the project pauses!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the string and duration parameters for each sayText function, then use a pause function set to the same duration?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What messages might be shared in each sayText?

❓ Did you match the pause parameter to the same value as the duration parameter in each sayText?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to place quotation marks around each of the strings and to test out the project to make sure the messages appear as intended.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to share directions with the user after the sprites disappear!


Open Sprites and drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the for element of loop. Update the sprite name, string parameter, and the duration parameter, so that the Player sprite asks the user where the sprites went. 


Add another [(this) say (:))] underneath the sayText code. Update the sprite name, the string parameter, and  the duration parameter so that the Player sprite tells the user to press the A button to tell what they saw.


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] below each sayText. Set the parameter to the same value used in each duration parameter of the sayText functions. 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite give the user directions after the hiding sprites disappear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a userGuess variable and set it to the game.askForString function inside the controller.A event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the userGuess variable be used for?

❓ What might you use as the message parameter in the askForString code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that when they are setting the answerLength parameter in the askForString code they should make sure it is as long as the longest variable’s name in each array.

💡 The userGuess variable will be used to store user input, which can be used to match the values in each array.
steps.instructions:
Ask the user to share a sprite they saw on screen when the A button is pressed!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on A button pressed. Use the default property A and default event Pressed.


Inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event, declare a new variable called userGuess. Open Game, then drag [ask for string] to the right of the assignment operator. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.askForString(null) 

Update the message parameter, so that the project asks the user to name 1 sprite that they saw on screen. Update the answerLength parameter to limit how long the user’s answer can be.


Click ▶ then press the A button to see the project ask the user to name 1 sprite they saw.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare the userIndex variable and set it to use indexOf to compare elements in the oceanStrings array with the userGuess variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the userIndex variable be used for?

❓ What does the indexOf function do? What is it used for?

❓ How is the oceanStrings array and the userGuess variable used in the userIndex variable declaration?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The userIndex variable will be used to determine whether the user’s guess matches one of the sprites that appeared on the screen.

💡 The indexOf function returns the index of the first occurrence of a value in an array. In this example, the indexOf function is used to search the oceanStrings array for the first instance of the user-submitted string. If a matching string is present, the function will return the index of the element in the array. If there is not a matching string, the returned value will be -1.

💡 Point out to the ninja the need for both the oceanStrings and the oceanImages arrays. Because the user cannot submit an image, a string must be used to determine whether their guess matches a sprite on screen.
steps.instructions:
Compare the user’s guess with the elements in the array to check if they answered correctly! 


Underneath the userGuess variable, declare another variable called userIndex. To the right of the assignment operator, type oceanStrings followed by a dot operator, then select indexOf from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses ( ) with userGuess inside of them so that the code looks like:

let userIndex = oceanStrings.indexOf(userGuess) 

After each user guess, the code will search the oceanStrings array for a matching string. If a match is present, the variable will store the index value of the element, which will be a number greater than or equal to 0. If a match is not present, it will store the returned value -1.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace mySprite with oceanSprites[userindex] in both the setFlag and sayText functions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition needs to be true in order for the code inside the if conditional to run? 

❓ Why should oceanSprites[userindex] be used as the sprite name in both the setFlag and sayText functions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the userindex variable has a value greater than or equal to 0, then the code inside the if conditional will run. If this condition is true, the user has submitted a string that correctly matches a value in the oceanStrings array.

💡 oceanSprites[userindex] should be used as the sprite name in both the setFlag and sayText functions so that the correctly named sprite reappears and congratulates the user. The userindex variable matches the index of the correctly named string in the oceanStrings array with the corresponding sprite in the oceanSprites array.
steps.instructions:
Code the hiding sprite to reappear if the user guesses the sprite correctly!


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the userIndex variable. Inside the parentheses, replace true with code that checks if the value of the userIndex variable is greater than or equal to 0. 


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional. Replace mySprite with oceanSprites[userIndex], so that the setFlag function is applied to the user guessed sprite. Update the flag parameter by deleting .AutoDestroy, retyping the dot operator, then selecting Invisible from the code completion tool. Change the on parameter to false, to turn the sprite flag off so the sprite will reappear.


Open Sprites and drag [(this) say (:))] underneath the setFlag code, inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional. Replace mySprite with oceanSprites[userIndex], then update the string and duration parameters so that the sprite tells the user that they guessed correctly. 


Click ▶ to see the correctly guessed sprite reappear and congratulate the user!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use removeAt to remove the sprite from both the oceanSprites and oceanStrings arrays?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the removeAt function do? How is it used?

❓ Why does the value of userIndex need to be removed from both oceanStrings and oceanSprites arrays?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The removeAt function removes an element at a certain index of an array. In this example, the function is used to remove the element at the index, determined by the value of userIndex, in both oceanStrings and oceanSprites arrays.

💡 The correctly named sprite, or the element at the index of userIndex, needs to be removed from both arrays to keep them in sync. Only removing the correctly named sprite from 1 of the arrays will result in errors when comparing the 2 arrays, such as a non-matching image appearing after a user submits a string.
steps.instructions:
Remove the sprite from each array, once the user has guessed it correctly!


Inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional and below the sayText code, type oceanSprites followed by a dot operator. Select removeAt from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses ( ) with the userIndex variable inside so that the code looks like: 

oceanSprites.removeAt(userIndex) 

Copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) the removeAt code on a new line below it. Update the array selected by changing oceanSprites to oceanStrings.


Now, if the user guesses a sprite correctly, the sprite and its name will be removed from both the oceanSprites and oceanStrings arrays. In order to keep the index of the sprites and their names the same in each array, the sprite value needs to be removed from both arrays.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an if conditional and oceanSprites.length to check whether all of the sprites have been guessed correctly?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition needs to be true in order for the game to end in a win?

❓ When will the length of the oceanSprites array equal 0?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The game will end in a win once the the length of the oceanSprites array is equal to 0. This will happen once the user has correctly named all of the sprites and have been removed from the oceanSprites array.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
End the game if the user guesses all of the sprites correctly!


Open Logic and drag [if] underneath the conditional inside the controller.A event. Inside the parentheses, replace true with code that checks if all of the values in the oceanSprites array have been removed. 


Type oceanSprites followed by a dot operator. Select the length property from the code completion tool. Then, use an equality operator == to check if the length of the oceanSprites array is equal to 0.


Add a pause inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional. Update the parameter so that the project pauses briefly before ending. Then, open Game and drag [game over (true)] underneath. Change the win parameter to true.


Click ▶ to see the project end in a win when the user correctly guesses all of the sprites on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help users understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background image might you use to show an aquatic scene?

❓ What screen effect might be used to enhance the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they might select a screen effect that matches the project’s scene, such as bubbles.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background image, screen effect, and directions!


Open Scene and drag [set background image to (img)] above the Player sprite’s code under // game set up. Select an aquatic scene background image from the gallery.


Open Scene again and drag [start screen (effect) effect] under // game set up. Use the dot operator . to access the list of possible effects in the code completion tool. 


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] on a blank line between the Player sprite’s code and the for loop. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box invites the user to explore all of the sprites together.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses the index of elements in an array to trigger different things to happen.

validationItems.text: Create an oceanImages array to contain 4 sprite image variables and an oceanStrings array to contain their names.
Use a for loop to create sprites from the images and give them random positions.
Create an empty oceanSprites array and add the sprites created in the for loop to the array.
Use a for element loop to set each ocean sprite’s Invisible flag to true.
Use pause and sayText to give directions to the player.
Ask the user for a string when the A button is pressed. Store the value in a userGuess variable.
Use the indexOf function to find the user’s guess in the oceanStrings array, inside the button pressed event.
Make a sprite appear if the user guessed correctly
Use the removeAt function to remove the sprite and string from both arrays if the user guessed correctly.
End the game if the user guesses all the sprites correctly.
Add a background image, screen effects, and directions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about arrays and several functions available to help you create and update arrays in JavaScript. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Making a List, Checking it Twice
badges.description: Create and modify arrays within a program in JavaScript.

badges.title: Array of Sunshine
badges.description: Create an array in JavaScript.

badges.title: A Lengthy Calculation
badges.description: Calculate the length of an array.

badges.title: I Choose You!
badges.description: Access an element based on its index in an array.

badges.title: Objects May Be Larger Than They Appear
badges.description: Change the scale of a sprite.

badges.title: You’ll Fit Right In
badges.description: Use the push function to add an element to the end of an array.

badges.title: A String of Questions
badges.description: Use the askForString function to prompt the user for a string response.

badges.title: For Each Its Own
badges.description: Use a for element of loop to iterate through all the elements in an array.

badges.title: Search Engine
badges.description: Use the indexOf function to find the index of a provided value in an array.

badges.title: You’re Outta Here
badges.description: Use the removeAt function to remove a specific element from an array.
